t: Max Chunks To Make Sorted II — Editorial
o: We must partition `arr` into consecutive chunks so that sorting each chunk and concatenating yields the fully sorted array, maximizing the chunk count. A cut after index `i` is valid exactly when the multiset of `arr[0..i]` equals the multiset of the smallest `i+1` values of the array. In example 1 (`[5,4,3,2,1]`) no prefix ever matches a sorted prefix, so the answer is 1. In example 2 (`[2,1,3,4,4]`), cuts after indices 1, 2, 3 are all valid (prefixes `[2,1]`, `[2,1,3]`, `[2,1,3,4]` match sorted prefixes), giving 4 chunks. With n up to 2000 an O(n²) check per cut is fine, but O(n log n) or O(n) solutions exist.
k: A cut at position i is valid iff max(arr[0..i]) <= min(arr[i+1..n-1]).
Equivalently, sort the array; scan left to right tracking running prefix sums of arr and sorted arr — every point where they're equal is a valid cut.
A monotonic stack can track chunk boundaries: merge chunks whenever a new element is smaller than the current chunk's max.

a.n: Approach 1: Prefix Max vs Suffix Min
a.i: For each split point i, the chunk boundary works iff everything on the left is ≤ everything on the right. Precompute `leftMax[i] = max(arr[0..i])` and `rightMin[i] = min(arr[i..n-1])`. Then count positions where `leftMax[i] <= rightMin[i+1]`; each such position ends a chunk. This directly encodes the validity condition with no sorting needed.
s: Build leftMax in one pass from the left.
Build rightMin in one pass from the right.
Scan i from 0 to n-2; increment answer when leftMax[i] <= rightMin[i+1].
Add 1 for the final chunk and return.
a.t: O(n) — three linear passes over the array.
a.sp: O(n) — two auxiliary arrays of size n.

a.i: Sort a copy of the array. A cut after index i is valid iff the first i+1 elements of `arr` are exactly the first i+1 elements of the sorted array as multisets. Comparing running sums detects this: since all elements are non-negative, equal prefix sums plus equal lengths imply equal multisets. Every time the running sums coincide, we can close a chunk.
s: Copy and sort the array into `sortedArr`.
Iterate i, maintaining running sums `sumA` of arr and `sumS` of sortedArr.
When sumA == sumS, increment the chunk count.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting; the scan is O(n).
a.sp: O(n) — the sorted copy of the array.

a.i: Process elements left to right, treating the stack as holding the maximum of each current chunk. If the incoming element is ≥ the stack top, it starts a new chunk. Otherwise it must belong to an earlier chunk: pop all stack tops greater than it, then push back the largest popped value so that chunk's max is preserved. The final stack size equals the number of chunks.
s: For each element x: while the stack top > x, pop and remember the max popped value m.
Push back max(m, x) if anything was popped; otherwise push x.
a.t: O(n) — each element is pushed and popped at most once.
a.sp: O(n) — the stack in the worst case (sorted input).

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1 (prefix max / suffix min) since its correctness argument is the simplest, then mention Approach 2's elegant sorted-prefix-sum trick or Approach 3's monotonic stack as refinements. Pitfalls: forgetting to use `<=` (not `<`) when comparing leftMax and rightMin — duplicates spanning a boundary are allowed; using 32-bit sums in Java/C++ for Approach 2 (values up to 1e8 times n=2000 exceeds int range); off-by-one errors ensuring the last element always closes a chunk. Edge cases: single-element arrays (answer 1), all-equal arrays (answer n), strictly decreasing arrays (answer 1). Follow-ups often include LeetCode 769 (the permutation-only variant solvable by comparing running max to index), or asking for the minimum number of chunks instead.
